title: The Castro Essays
text:
In 1967 Edward Jones and Victor Harris of Duke University asked students to read a short essay about Fidel Castro's Cuba, at a time when Cold War feelings ran high in the United States. Some essays were in favor of Castro and some were against.

Half of the readers were told that the writer had chosen which side to argue. The other half were told that the writer had been assigned the position by a debate coach or instructor, and had no choice. The readers then estimated the writer's true attitude toward Castro.

When the writer had chosen freely, readers naturally assumed the essay reflected his opinion. The surprise came in the no-choice condition. Even though readers knew the writer had simply been told which side to argue, they still rated the author of a pro-Castro essay as considerably more favorable to Castro than the author of an anti-Castro essay. They gave too little weight to the situation and too much to the person.

The tendency to explain other people's behavior by their character while overlooking the pressures of their circumstances was later named the fundamental attribution error by Lee Ross. It has been found in many settings, though it appears stronger in some cultures than in others.
lesson: People's actions often reflect their circumstances more than their character. Before judging someone, ask what role or pressure might be shaping what they did.
source: Jones, E. E., and Harris, V. A. (1967). The attribution of attitudes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 3(1), 1-24.
